    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that there’s a newly introduced vibe-coded OS in town going by the name of LiberNT.
    • Industry observers note that liberNT has been under development for some time, but on Wednesday it made a substantial leap.
    • This still fledgling operating system is designed (mostly) for modern hardware and focuses on 64-bit platforms: amd64, arm64 and riscv64.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that there’s a newly introduced vibe-coded OS in town going by the name of LiberNT. Its name provides a big clue to its nature: Liber (free), NT (New Technology architecture, as in Windows NT). As it has been released under GNU’s GPL3.0 license, LiberNT also provides a free new way to run apps designed for Microsoft’s Windows 11.

    Industry observers note that liberNT has been under development for some time, but on Wednesday it made a substantial leap. Reading the intro, you might have wondered if this work had a ReactOS connection, and indeed there is. But what started as a fork of ReactOS has already got a fresh boot loader, graphics stack, memory manager – and yesterday a new kernel. “LiberNT is not affiliated with or endorsed by the ReactOS project or Microsoft,” insist the devs behind this OS.

    This still fledgling operating system is designed (mostly) for modern hardware and focuses on 64-bit platforms: amd64, arm64 and riscv64. Ambitiously, the goal is to develop this OS to deliver a free Windows alternative that is “stable, reliable and efficient.” On that latter point, yesterday’s blog revision relays some impressive efficiency and performance stats.

    In a recent development, the LiberNT team has benchmarked their eponymous OS against Microsoft’s Windows NT, and it beats it hands-down in 112 of 132 system tests. The testing assessed performance in the following areas: file caching, memory handling, threads and locks, plus FAT32 and NTFS storage. Interestingly, both the free and commercial OS were benchmarked on a Mac with an Apple M3 Pro chip. We scanned through the results, and the worst loss for LiberNT was a 28% performance deficit vs Win11, but it claims some astounding relative performance wins showing the free OS being over 2000% faster.

    The devs are entirely clear about the fact that the operating system was vibe coded. “AI is part of how LiberNT is built. It helps us review and write code, and everything it writes is then reviewed by a human,” explains a section of the GitHub page for the project. “Before anything reaches the main branch, a person runs and validates the end-to-end tests. We care about this project too much to let a regression slip through.”.

    It has been revealed that if the above highlights about this new OS's scope, mission, compatibility, and performance have whetted your appetite, there is the full code available via the GitHub link (top), and even some ready-made builds as bootable disk images. Indeed, I’m quite eager to give this new OS a spin. Hopefully, it works as well as the ambitious developers suggest, and I won’t be disappointed by any stability concerns using my daily productivity apps like Firefox, Word, and an old release of Photoshop.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

    Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half

    📅 11 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.
    • Researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy.
    • Recent findings suggest that in the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.

    Researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy. The breakthrough was published in the scientific journalScience Advances.

    Recent findings suggest that in the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip. Instead of moving information around a chip with electrical signals, devices could transmit data using photons, the particles that make up light.

    "The nanolaser opens up the possibility of creating a new generation of components that combine high performance with minimal size. This could be in information technology, for example, where ultra-small and energy-efficient lasers can reduce energy consumption in computers, or in the development of sensors for the healthcare sector, where the nanolaser's extreme light concentration can deliver high-resolution images and ultrasensitive biosensors," claims DTU professor Jesper Mørk.

    Mørk co-authored the study with, among others, Drs. Meng Xiong and Yi Yu from DTU Electro.

    Using Light Inside Computer Chips.

    Recent findings suggest that much of the internet already relies on light to carry information through fiber optic cables. Inside computers, however, data still moves through electronic circuits using electricity. That approach produces heat and can limit how quickly information can be transferred.

    According to recent reports, nanolasers could bring optical communication directly onto microchips. By generating light signals efficiently inside the chip, they could allow information to move with very little energy loss, potentially making future devices faster, cooler, and more energy efficient.

    Mørk estimates that using nanolasers in computers could reduce energy consumption by as much as half.

    The compact DTU nanolaser is an crucial step toward that goal. Future chips designed around light-based communication would likely require thousands of extremely small, efficient lasers working together to transmit information across the chip.

    Breaking the Size Limit for Lasers.

    It has been revealed that the newly introduced nanolaser was created in DTU's clean room facility, DTU Nanolab. According to Mørk, the device pushes beyond the conventional limit for how small a laser can be made.

    Sources indicate that at its core is a structure known as a nanocavity, which traps and concentrates light within an exceptionally tiny space. Until now, achieving such intense confinement at this scale had been considered extremely difficult.

    When researchers shine a beam of light onto the device, both photons and electrons become concentrated in the same microscopic region. This interaction allows the laser to function at room temperature while requiring unusually little energy.

    The light-trapping structure used in the nanolaser was originally developed by Professor Ole Sigmund's group at DTU Construct.

    Faster Devices and Lower Energy Use.

    It has been revealed that the next major challenge is making the nanolaser operate using electrical power. If researchers can achieve that, the technology could have broad applications across computing, communications, and healthcare.

    It has been revealed that computers and smartphones could potentially deliver greater performance while consuming less electricity. Data centers, which require enormous amounts of power, could also see substantial reductions in energy use, potentially leading to significant climate benefits.

    In healthcare technology, the nanolaser's ability to concentrate light into an extremely small area could support ultra-sensitive sensors and high-resolution imaging systems.

    Researchers estimate that the remaining technical challenges could be solved within the next 5-10 years.

    In a recent development, materials provided by Technical University of Denmark. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, more information about the alleged knowledge of chip diversion by a Supermicro executive is being revealed as shareholders’ civil lawsuit against the tech giant progresses. According to The Telegraph, the investors alleged that there was “no way Cenly Chen lacked knowledge about the company’s illicit sales.” Chen, the former Chief Growth Officer at Supermicro and described by a colleague as the company’s sales leader, resigned from her position in April of this year — about a month after the three Supermicro employees, including its co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, were arrested for a $2.5-billion AI GPU smuggling scheme.

    Cenly Chen is married to former Nvidia Executive Vice President of Worldwide Field Operations Jay Puri, who is also described as the organization’s sales chief. The Information also called him Jensen Huang’s right-hand man and mentioned he was the person that Nvidia’s customers turned to if they wanted to buy chips or had other pressing concerns. The shareholders’ accusations and her relationship with Puri have put the former Supermicro executive in the spotlight, especially after Huang’s sudden departure from the AI chipmaker amid a flurry of affairs and smuggling accusations.

    Sources say that Puri controlled the AI chip allocations to server manufacturers, including Supermicro, while the lawsuit claims that Chen decided how many Nvidia racks each Supermicro customer could get. A former Supermicro employee was also quoted in the complaint saying that it was “widely known within the Organization that Chen had to leave because she had sent emails requesting that Nvidia release chips with serial numbers associated with the GPUs illegally diverted to customers in China.” This apparently refers to the serial numbers that were moved from real to dummy servers using a hairdryer.

    Supermicro has remarked multiple times that it has cooperated with the U.S. government regarding the smuggling investigation and that it has not been included in the lawsuit against the three defendants. Furthermore, the firm has denied her involvement regarding Nvidia GPU allocations. “Chen did not manage Supermicro’s relationship with Nvidia and did not decide how Nvidia GPUs were distributed to customers,” a Supermicro spokesperson told The Information. They also said that she left voluntarily and that her LinkedIn profile now reads her current position as CEO of ChronoScale, an Nvidia cloud partner based in Silicon Valley. As for Puri, he stepped away from his position at Nvidia in late August, about two months before the Jensen Huang scandal blew up, although he remains as an advisor to the AI chipmaker.

    Taco Bell is bringing back a discontinued menu item after a decade, with the fast-food chain confirming that one of its former burritos will return to restaurants nationwide in 2027.

    The announcement comes as Taco Bell continues to revive older menu items, including the Quesarito, Flamin’ Hot Grilled Cheese Burrito, and Cheesy Street Chalupas, which have recently returned for limited-time runs.

    It has been revealed that however, the latest comeback wasn’t decided by Taco Bell executives. Instead, the company allowed fans to choose which discontinued item would return as part of its inaugural Live Más Open golf tournament, hosted by comedian Kevin Hart.

    Taco Bell has confirmed that the Steakhouse Boss Burrito will return to participating US restaurants for a limited time in 2027, marking its first appearance since 2016.

    Originally introduced as the Steakhouse Burrito, the returning item features a warm flour tortilla filled with a choice of grilled, marinated steak or marinated all-white-meat chicken.

    The burrito includes twice the amount of meat found in Taco Bell’s Steak Grilled Cheese Burrito, along with warm queso sauce, bacon, seasoned potatoes, and reduced-fat sour cream.

    It also features a three-cheese blend consisting of mozzarella, pepper jack, and cheddar.

    The decision to bring back the burrito came during Taco Bell’s Live Más Open, which took place at The Ranch at Laguna Beach in California earlier this month.

    The nine-hole golf tournament featured celebrities, athletes, and Taco Bell fans competing for the opportunity to revive a discontinued menu item.

    The Live Más Open is available to stream on Peacock beginning November 20, with a television broadcast scheduled for November 23 on Golf Channel.

    • Recent findings suggest that the findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Artificial intelligence is giving researchers a upcoming way to listen to what patients are saying about popular GLP-1 drugs. After analyzing more than 400,000 Reddit posts, a University of Pennsylvania team identified several symptoms reported by people using semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound) that may not be fully represented in clinical trials or official regulatory information.

    Recent findings suggest that the study, published recently in Nature Health, examined more than five years of posts from nearly 70,000 Reddit people. Two categories stood out as particularly deserving of further investigation: reproductive symptoms, including changes in menstrual cycles, and problems involving body temperature, such as chills and hot flashes.

    Recent findings suggest that the findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms. Instead, researchers say the massive collection of spontaneous patient reports may reveal signals worth examining more closely.

    According to recent reports, "Some of the side effects we found, like nausea, are well known, and that indicates that the method is picking up a real signal," notes Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS) at Penn Engineering and the study's senior author. "The underreported symptoms are leads that came from patients themselves, unprompted, and clinicians could potentially pay attention to them.".

    What Patients Report Outside Clinical Trials.

    Clinical trials are designed to determine whether treatments work and to identify important safety problems, but they cannot necessarily capture every symptom that matters to patients once a medication is being used by a much larger population.

    Recent findings suggest that "Clinical trials generally identify the most dangerous side effects of drugs," adds Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author on the study. "But they can fail to find what symptoms patients are most concerned about; even though social media is not necessarily representative, a large collection of posts may reflect additional concerns.".

    According to recent reports, the distinction is crucial. The study found associations in what people discussed online, not proof that GLP-1 drugs were responsible for those experiences.

    "We can't say that GLP-1s are actually causing these symptoms," notes Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS advised by Guntuku and Ungar. "But nearly 4% of the Reddit consumers in our sample reported menstrual irregularities, which would be even higher in a female-only sample. We think that's a signal worth investigating.".

    Using Social Media as an Early Health Signal.

    It has been revealed that the idea of mining online conversations for clues about drug safety predates today's AI boom. In 2011, Ungar participated in one of the earliest efforts to use material created by internet users to identify possible adverse effects from medications.

    Social media can capture experiences that patients discuss with one another but may never formally report to a doctor, drug manufacturer, or regulator.

    "Online patient communities work a lot like a neighborhood grapevine," says Ungar. "People who are living with these medications are swapping notes with each other in real time, sharing experiences that rarely make it into a doctor's office visit or an official report.".

    According to recent reports, since then, online patient communities have expanded enormously. That has made social media a potentially valuable source for studying how medications affect people in everyday life, although gaining access to platform data has become more difficult.

    Traditional clinical research remains essential, the researchers emphasize, but online conversations can provide information far more rapidly when millions of people begin using a drug.

    Sources indicate that "Clinical trials are the gold standard, but by design, they are slow," says Guntuku. "This is not a replacement for trials, but it can move much faster, and that speed matters when a drug goes from niche to mainstream almost overnight.".

    AI Makes Massive Social Media Analysis Possible.

    One of the biggest obstacles has always been scale.

    Guntuku describes the approach as "computational social listening," which uses computational methods to identify patterns in large collections of online conversations about health.

    Patients, however, rarely describe symptoms using standardized medical terminology. One person might describe feeling unusually cold, another might mention constant chills, while a clinician could categorize those experiences using a specific medical term.

    Researchers therefore need a way to translate everyday language into standardized categories. One key reference is the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA), which provides terminology widely used to classify medical conditions, symptoms, and adverse events.

    Previously, connecting huge numbers of informal social media posts with standardized medical terminology required enormous amounts of work, limiting how much data researchers could realistically analyze.

    Large language models such as GPT and Gemini are changing that equation by allowing researchers to process and categorize vast amounts of text more consistently and promptly.

    "Large language models have made it possible to do this kind of analysis much faster with a level of standardization that could be difficult to achieve before," notes Sehgal.

    Unexpected Symptoms Emerge From 400,000 Posts.

    The researchers stress that Reddit owners do not represent the overall population of people taking GLP-1 drugs. Reddit users tend to be younger, are more likely to be male, and are disproportionately located in the United States.

    Industry observers note that even with that limitation, the analysis produced a reassuring sign that the approach was detecting genuine patterns. Many of the symptoms discussed by Reddit owners closely matched already known effects of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

    Industry observers note that about 44% of consumers included in the study described at least one side effect. Gastrointestinal problems were the most common, consistent with the nausea and other digestive challenges already associated with these medications.

    More intriguing were symptoms that appeared frequently enough to attract the researchers' attention but may not be as well represented in current drug labels or conventional adverse event reports.

    In a recent development, nearly 4% of users who reported side effects described reproductive symptoms. These included changes in menstruation such as bleeding between periods, heavy bleeding, and irregular menstrual cycles.

    Owners also described changes involving body temperature, including chills, feeling unusually cold, hot flashes, and symptoms resembling a fever.

    According to recent reports, fatigue was another notable finding. It was the second most frequently reported complaint in the Reddit data, even though relatively few clinical trials reported fatigue often enough for it to reach established reporting thresholds.

    Why Menstrual and Temperature Changes Are Interesting.

    Sources indicate that one possible reason these reports caught researchers' attention involves the hypothalamus, a small but extremely notable region of the brain. Among its many jobs, the hypothalamus helps regulate hunger, hormones, reproduction and body temperature.

    "These drugs are thought to work by engaging part of the brain called the hypothalamus, which helps regulate a wide variety of hormones," claims Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study. "That doesn't mean the medications are necessarily causing these symptoms, but it could suggest that reports of menstrual changes and body temperature fluctuations are worth studying more systematically.".

    Sources indicate that the researchers are not proposing that this biological connection proves GLP-1 drugs are responsible. Instead, it offers another reason to test the patient-reported patterns more carefully through controlled research.

    Turning Online Conversations Into Research Leads.

    For now, the team hopes the results encourage scientists and clinicians to pay closer attention to symptoms that patients repeatedly discuss online.

    "They're clearly on patients' minds, and that's worth paying attention to," notes Sehgal.

    According to recent reports, the researchers also want to broaden their analysis beyond Reddit and beyond English-language communities. Doing so could help determine whether the same patterns emerge among different groups of people and on different social media platforms.

    "We don't really know yet whether what we're seeing on Reddit reflects the experience of GLP-1 users globally, or whether it's particular to the kind of person who posts on Reddit in the United States," Ungar states.

    In the longer term, rapid AI analysis of online patient conversations could potentially become an early detection system for emerging health concerns involving drugs, supplements and wellness products.

    That could be particularly valuable for substances that become popular online faster than conventional research can keep up. Loosely regulated or unregulated products, including injectable peptides, can spread promptly through communities on Reddit, TikTok and other platforms. Discussions among users may therefore provide some of the earliest indications of unexpected effects.

    "The whole point of this kind of approach is that it can move rapidly, and that's exactly when it's most valuable," states Guntuku.

    This study was conducted at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science. The authors report no outside funding. Tronieri reports receiving an investigator-initiated grant, on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, from Novo Nordisk and receiving consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. The other authors report no conflicts of interest.

    According to recent reports, intel has reduced its workforce by approximately 27,800 employees under Lip-Bu Tan, based on the firm's reported headcount figures, but this does not seem to be enough. The company has reportedly initiated another round of layoffs, this time across its global information technology (IT) organization, as its chief executive continues to reduce expenses and simplify the company's operations, reports Business Insider.

    The latest cuts in Intel's IT organization reportedly began on November 16, although Intel has not disclosed how many employees will lose their jobs, notes TrendForce citing CTech. Some employees claim that the reductions could affect a double-digit percentage of the department's workforce of around 2,607 people at 55 sites in 53 countries, so we are talking about at least 260 people if we are talking about a 10% reduction, or as much as 520 if we are talking about a 20% reduction. One has to keep in mind that these estimates have not been independently verified. Intel has neither confirmed the number of affected employees nor identified the specific teams involved. Instead, the firm reiterated to Business Insider that it regularly reviews its workforce to ensure that personnel and financial resources correspond to its strategic priorities.

    In a recent development, the latest reductions follow several rounds of layoffs throughout 2026. In July, Intel eliminated positions in its Data Center and AI Group. Between July and October, the organization submitted nine Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) notices in California, which covered 222 employees, according to Business Insider. The most recent notice, filed on October 22, concerned 67 permanent job cuts at Intel's Folsom campus (which mostly specializes in R&D, hardware validation, and software development), effective October 31. As of November 17, no additional WARN notices had been reported.

    Intel employed 81,100 people as of September 27, 2026, including 76,500 employees at Intel itself and another 4,600 at Mobileye and other subsidiaries. This compares with 85,100 employees at the end of 2025 and 108,900 a year earlier, which means that the company's workforce declined by 4,000 since December, 2025, and 27,800 since December, 2024. respectively.

    Intel's workforce reductions began well before Lip-Bu Tan became chief executive in 2025. In 2024, his predecessor Pat Gelsinger unveiled plans to eliminate more than 15,000 positions, or approximately 15% of the organization’s workforce. Tan has continued to reduce expenses, eliminate management layers, and discontinue lower-priority projects as Intel attempts to cut costs and reduce losses/improve profitability.

    Tech Report: The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange new physics

    📅 15 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics.
    • Recent findings suggest that in a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics.
    • The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics. Researchers have found that structures based on the shape can make light form unusual chiral patterns, pointing to fresh ways of exploring how geometry can influence optical behavior.

    Recent findings suggest that in a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics. When the team illuminated the structures with laser light, they observed diffraction effects unlike those seen in conventional quasicrystals.

    The Shape That Solved the Einstein Problem.

    The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.

    Sources indicate that familiar tilings such as checkerboards and honeycombs repeat in a regular way. An aperiodic monotile, by contrast, can fill a surface without ever settling into a repeating arrangement.

    In a recent development, in 2023, researchers discovered the first such monotile, the Smith hat. The finding attracted widespread attention because it provided a long-sought solution to the mathematical problem.

    Industry observers note that "What is especially fascinating about the hat tile is that, although the resulting pattern appears irregular at first glance, it is actually constructed from the honeycomb lattice," indicates lead author Yuto Moritake. "We wanted to see whether this unique shape could also produce any unexpected physical phenomena.".

    Turning a Mathematical Pattern Into an Optical Structure.

    To test that possibility, the researchers created nanoscale versions of the pattern on silicon nitride films using electron beam lithography.

    In a recent development, when laser light was directed at the structures, the resulting diffraction patterns formed distinctive pinwheel-like shapes. These patterns directly revealed the chiral character of the aperiodic structure.

    Chirality refers to a form of handedness in which a structure and its mirror image cannot be perfectly matched. In this case, the unusual arrangement of the monotile pattern caused the light itself to display a chiral response.

    In a recent development, "We found that the diffraction patterns themselves become chiral because the structure lacks mirror symmetry," explains senior author Masaya Notomi. "This kind of optical response is fundamentally different from that observed in conventional quasicrystalline materials.".

    Light Responds to Direction and Polarization.

    The researchers also found that the diffraction pattern changed depending on both the direction and polarization of the incoming light.

    When the physical structures were mirrored, their optical behavior reversed as well. This showed that the response of the light was directly tied to the symmetry of the underlying pattern, revealing a upcoming type of symmetry-controlled optical behavior.

    "These results open a new direction of research on the fusion of quasiperiodic order and chirality," remarks Moritake. "Monotile patterns provide a platform for exploring optical phenomena that emerge from the interplay of symmetry, chirality, and aperiodicity.".

    From Abstract Mathematics to New Optical Physics.

    The researchers say structures inspired by monotiles could eventually contribute to technologies designed to manipulate light, control polarization, and support advanced optical devices.

    Industry observers note that more broadly, the findings show how a discovery that began as an abstract mathematical puzzle can lead to unexpected physical effects. The Smith hat was first celebrated for solving a question about how shapes can cover a surface. Now, its unusual geometry may also help researchers uncover new ways to control and study light.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the AI data center build-out is pushing electricity grids across the globe, with many regions facing demand from projects that would exceed the current peak load that each system could support.
    • This massive power consumption is one of the reasons for the opposition against their construction in communities, with residents blaming them for increased utility prices.
    • It has been revealed that emissions are another issue that the IEA has raised.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the AI data center build-out is pushing electricity grids across the globe, with many regions facing demand from projects that would exceed the current peak load that each system could support. According to the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2026 report, a total of 120GW of capacity is right now available across all types of data centers across the globe, with another 120GW expected to be completed by the end of the decade, 75% of which would be dedicated to artificial intelligence. Aside from that, it’s also tracking 93 large “AI factories” that are either under construction or being expanded via satellite imagery. It estimates that the capacity for these sites grew from under 2GW to 17GW in just two years, and that they’re expected to hit a total of 50GW upon completion, the equivalent of adding a second Great Britain to power demand.

    This massive power consumption is one of the reasons for the opposition against their construction in communities, with residents blaming them for increased utility prices. However, the IEA states that its analysis “does not yet show a clear relationship between growth in data center capacity and increases in electricity prices.” It noted that if a data center uses existing capacity and pays for its share of the cost, then it could potentially lead to lower utility bills for all customers. However, if the grid operator is required to upgrade its system to accommodate the large consumer, then it could also lead to increased monthly bills if the costs are spread across all users.

    It has been revealed that emissions are another issue that the IEA has raised. Renewable energy dominates data centers’ power purchase agreements at nearly 50%, but actual power generation puts coal- and natural-gas power sources closer to 60%. This is likely due to the need for reliability, with the latter kicking in when the former cannot deliver the power that the data center needs. Aside from that, a few projects are deploying their own power, like Elon Musk’s Colossus 2 in Southaven, Mississippi, with about 180GW planned or under construction in the U.S. So, even though renewable energy is growing to accommodate demand, it’s also expected that coal- and natural-gas emissions from data centers will rise by 70% by 2030.

    It has been revealed that investments in AI data centers are expected to hit $32 trillion by 2050, putting the infrastructure spending for the industry larger than railways, electrification, and the internet, combined. Despite that, the IEA notes the grid remains a significant bottleneck — renewable power plants take between one and five years to complete, which is around the same time that some massive data center projects take if they do not face an extended moratorium, while transmission works can take three to five times longer. This is probably one of the reasons why some AI hyperscalers are choosing to put jet engines on their sites instead, although these are also facing shortages, especially in turbine blades.

    Now that GTA 6 is out on PlayStation and Xbox, players on the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit have gone back through the post and say its ending details match the final game.

    It added that the game was “still in the very early stages of development, though, it’ll probably be 2030 when it comes out.”.

    The source also claimed Rockstar wants to bring back the facial-scanning tech the original LA Noire was known for, and push it much further than seen previously.

    According to recent reports, “The higher-ups are talking about doing the face scanning stuff again, but making it insane. They want it to be the best looking game ever made,” the post said.

    Sources indicate that the rumor first did the rounds in September 2026, before the GTA 6 details could be checked against the finished game. None of the LA Noire 2 claims have been confirmed.

    Rockstar hasn’t revealed what Rockstar Australia is working on, and has yet to announce a fresh LA Noire game.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes. Because of their small size, these robotic insects could potentially move through narrow spaces that larger drones cannot enter while avoiding walls, debris, and falling objects.

    Recent findings suggest that until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them. They typically moved slowly and followed relatively simple flight paths.

    Researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a fresh approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility. The team developed an AI-based controller that allows the robotic bug to perform demanding aerial maneuvers, including repeated body flips.

    Using a two-part control system designed to balance performance with computational efficiency, the researchers increased the robot's speed by about 450 percent and its acceleration by about 250 percent compared with their previous best results.

    The robot was agile enough to complete 10 consecutive somersaults in 11 seconds, even while wind disturbances tried to knock it away from its intended path.

    Industry observers note that "We want to be able to use these robots in scenarios that more traditional quadcopter robots would have trouble flying into, but that insects could navigate. Now, with our bioinspired control framework, the flight performance of our robot is comparable to insects in terms of speed, acceleration, and the pitching angle. This is quite an exciting step toward that future goal," claims Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-senior author of a paper on the robot.

    Chen is joined on the paper by co-lead authors Yi-Hsuan Hsiao, an EECS MIT graduate student; Andrea Tagliabue PhD '24; and Owen Matteson, a graduate student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro); as well as EECS graduate student Suhan Kim; Tong Zhao MEng '23; and co-senior author Jonathan P. How, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). The research was published in Science Advances.

    AI Gives the Robot a Smarter Flight Controller.

    Chen's group has spent more than five years developing robotic insects.

    Recent findings suggest that the team recently created a more durable version of their tiny robot, which is about the size of a microcassette and weighs less than a paperclip. This newer design has larger flapping wings that support more agile flight. The wings are driven by soft artificial muscles that contract rapidly enough to produce extremely fast wingbeats.

    Industry observers note that the physical design had improved, but the robot's controller remained a major limitation. This controller acts as the robot's "brain," determining where the robot is and deciding how it should move. In earlier versions, a human had to tune the controller by hand.

    For the robot to fly with the speed and aggressiveness of a real insect, the researchers needed a system that could handle uncertainty while rapidly solving complex control problems.

    A controller powerful enough to do that would normally demand too much computation to operate in real time, especially because the aerodynamics of such a lightweight flying machine are highly complex.

    To solve this problem, Chen's group collaborated with How's team to develop a two-step AI-driven control system. The design combines the robustness needed for difficult, high-speed maneuvers with enough computational efficiency to work in real time.

    "The hardware advances pushed the controller so there was more we could do on the software side, but at the same time, as the controller developed, there was more they could do with the hardware. As Kevin's team demonstrates new capabilities, we demonstrate that we can utilize them," How says.

    Teaching a Tiny Robot to Plan Difficult Maneuvers.

    The first part of the system uses what is known as a model-predictive controller. This type of controller relies on a dynamic mathematical model to predict how the robot will behave and determine the best sequence of actions for safely following a desired flight path.

    Although this method requires substantial computing power, it can proposal difficult movements such as aerial flips, sharp turns, and aggressive changes in body angle. The planner also takes into account limits on the amount of force and torque the robot can produce, helping it avoid movements that could lead to a crash.

    Industry observers note that repeated flips are particularly challenging. To perform one somersault after another, the robot must slow down in exactly the right way so that it begins each new flip under the proper conditions.

    Industry observers note that "If small errors creep in, and you try to repeat that flip 10 times with those small errors, the robot will just crash. We need to have robust flight control," How notes.

    The researchers then used this expert planner to train a "policy" built on a deep-learning model through a process called imitation learning. The policy serves as the robot's real-time decision-making system, determining how and where it should fly.

    In effect, imitation learning allows the team to capture the behavior of the more computationally demanding controller in a faster AI model that can operate swiftly enough for real-time flight.

    A major part of the challenge was generating enough useful training data to teach the policy how to handle aggressive maneuvers without creating an unnecessarily large data set.

    "The robust training method is the secret sauce of this technique," How explains.

    During flight, the AI-based policy receives information about the robot's position and converts it into real-time commands controlling factors such as thrust force and torques.

    Sources indicate that experiments demonstrated that the two-step control system dramatically improved the robot's performance. The insect-scale machine flew 447 percent faster and achieved a 255 percent increase in acceleration.

    It also completed 10 somersaults in only 11 seconds while remaining within about 4 or 5 centimeters of its planned flight path.

    "This work demonstrates that soft and microrobots, traditionally limited in speed, can now leverage advanced control algorithms to achieve agility approaching that of natural insects and larger robots, opening up newly introduced opportunities for multimodal locomotion," says Hsiao.

    It has been revealed that the team also demonstrated a movement known as a saccade. In insects, this involves pitching the body sharply, rapidly moving to a latest position, and then pitching in the opposite direction to stop. This quick acceleration and braking can help insects determine their position and maintain clear vision.

    "This bio-mimicking flight behavior could help us in the future when we start putting cameras and sensors on board the robot," Chen says.

    Toward Autonomous Flying Microrobots.

    One major goal for future research is to equip the microrobots with onboard cameras and sensors. That could eventually allow them to fly outdoors without depending on a sophisticated external motion capture system.

    The team also plans to investigate whether onboard sensing could help groups of the robots avoid crashing into one another and coordinate their movements while navigating.

    "For the micro-robotics community, I hope this paper signals a paradigm shift by showing that we can develop a new control architecture that is high-performing and efficient at the same time," states Chen.

    This research is funded, in part, by the National Science Foundation (NSF), the Office of Naval Research, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and the Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, considering the current status of the cybersecurity landscape, some may well say that "0-day" has lost its meaning, The latest high-stakes vulnerability pertains to a bug in Windows 11 (and possibly 10), wherein an attacker can partially bypass the lock screen and run software as the logged-in user, and seemingly access their data. If true, the vulnerability means even BitLocker won't help keep owners' files protected.

    It has been revealed that unsurprisingly, the bug was discovered by Abdelhamid Naceri, the prolific Windows hacker known to the world as Nightmare Eclipse, and is responsible for about a dozen zero-day findings in Microsoft's operating system. The exploit requires physical access to the machine, but that's precisely the scenario that lock screens and/or BitLocker are supposed to protect against.

    Recent findings suggest that to trigger the vulnerability, all you need is a keyboard. In the Windows 11 lock screen, click "Forgot my PIN," then hit Win+U to bring up the voice narrator. The window will be hidden behind the lock screen, which, for practical purposes, is just a veneer, but you can interact with it using the keyboard if you hold down the Caps Lock key and use the arrows and Enter.

    After some brief navigation through Narrator, you'll actually be in Settings, and then have multiple avenues for further shenanigans. One obvious one is going into Bluetooth and Devices and setting Autoplay to show a USB stick's files and folders, then plugging in your own with your software of choice to run. Additionally, on a personal machine, the user is bound to have administrator permissions, so you can just create your own account.

    Sources indicate that this bug is quite fresh, so there isn't widespread reporting or testing. The author claims "the vulnerability seems to be extremely consistent in every machine I tested it in." We did encounter a sysadmin on Reddit, danrhodes1987, who claims they've tested it on machines they manage, and sure enough, it works, though only on their InTune-enrolled devices. He indicates that "you can launch anything you want in the context of the user logged onto the device.".

    Additionally, they found it possible to invisibly navigate whichever programs the user had open before they locked their screen, which all but guarantees that the victim's entire data and programs will be fully accessible. As a Windows sysadmin friend of mine remarked, Windows' lock screen implementation always felt like a kludge, and he posits this won't be the last hack found for it.

    #47100. Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

    📅 25 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1175 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

    Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

    📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1175 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software.
    • Scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons.
    • "We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," mentioned Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the latest study published in Nature.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software. Researchers have now demonstrated a upcoming way to reach that level of flexibility using unusual quantum objects known as non-Abelian anyons.

    Scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons. Their results provide the first experimental demonstration that this approach can support the broad range of operations required for universal quantum computing.

    "We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," mentioned Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the latest study published in Nature.

    A Possible Shortcut Around Costly Quantum Error Correction.

    The strategy could do more than help create a general-purpose quantum computer. It may also offer a more efficient route toward reliable quantum machines.

    It has been revealed that quantum computers are extremely vulnerable to errors, so researchers typically protect information by distributing it across many physical qubits. These error correction methods can preserve data, but they usually do not provide every operation needed to perform universal quantum computation on that protected information.

    To fill the gap, engineers often rely on specially prepared resources called "magic states." Producing them usually requires an intensive purification process known as distillation, which can consume a large fraction of a quantum computer's available qubits. The latest results suggest that non-Abelian anyons may offer a way around that expensive step.

    "Non-Abelian codes are a dark horse in the race to quantum error correction," stated Henrik Dreyer, managing director and scientific lead at Quantinuum's Munich office and a co-author of the study. "In this work we show the first universal gate set in a non-Abelian code, which demonstrates that fault-tolerant computations can in principle be done without resorting to magic state distillation or cultivation, which are the most expensive operations in standard quantum error correction codes.".

    Why Non-Abelian Anyons Are Different.

    According to recent reports, ordinary qubits encode information using two basic states, along with quantum combinations of those states. Non-Abelian anyons work in a fundamentally different way.

    In a recent development, these anyons do not appear as ordinary standalone particles in nature. Instead, scientists create them inside quantum circuits by entangling many conventional qubits into a collective state that behaves as though it were a new type of particle with its own unusual rules.

    "The way I think about these codes is they're creating little universes -- alternative universes, but ones that reflect some of the properties of our own," Verresen noted.

    Each non-Abelian anyon carries an internal state that changes when one anyon is moved around another in a process known as braiding. The sequence of those braiding operations matters (that's what non-Abelian means), allowing information to be encoded and manipulated in ways that are unavailable to ordinary particles.

    In a recent development, because the information is spread across many entangled qubits rather than stored in a single location, it can also be naturally protected from some of the small disturbances that frequently disrupt conventional qubits. Braiding the anyons can also perform computational operations.

    Why Braiding Alone Was Not Enough.

    In 2024, a research team that included Verresen used a Quantinuum trapped-ion computer to create anyons associated with a symmetry group called D4 -- the rotations and reflections that leave a square unchanged -- demonstrating this form of non-Abelian order on quantum hardware for the first time.

    That experiment indicated that the unusual particles could be created and manipulated, but braiding them alone was not sufficient to carry out every operation required for universal quantum computing.

    Sources indicate that "In that work, we didn't demonstrate that those emergent forces were enough to do quantum computation," said Verresen. "That particular universe we created was not powerful enough.".

    Fusion Unlocks Universal Quantum Operations.

    For the latest study, the researchers switched to another symmetry known as S3 -- the rotations and mirror-image flips that leave an equilateral triangle unchanged -- and created the corresponding anyons on Quantinuum's H2 trapped-ion processor using 54 entangled qubits.

    The S3 system had the properties needed for universal quantum computation, but only when braiding was combined with another operation called fusion. During fusion, two anyons are brought together and the resulting state is measured.

    The underlying concept was proposed theoretically in 2003 by Carlos Mochon, then a student of John Preskill at Caltech. Turning that theoretical idea into an experiment that could actually run on quantum hardware, however, required extensive additional theoretical and experimental work.

    The researchers used pairs of anyons to encode "topological qutrits" which store three possible levels of quantum information instead of the two levels used by ordinary qubits.

    In a recent development, by combining different braiding and fusion operations, the team demonstrated three key tools: one entangling gate produced through braiding and two different measurements created through fusion. Together, those operations can in principle produce any quantum operation, including operations that braiding alone could not achieve.

    Beyond their possible computing applications, these unusual quantum states could also help researchers investigate fundamental aspects of physics.

    "It is gratifying to see ideas we have spent our PhD work thinking about realized in the lab, and it has been made possible by remarkable advances in quantum hardware over the past few years," remarked Anasuya Lyons and Chiu Fan Bowen Lo, graduate students at Harvard University in the group of Ashvin Vishwanath who helped lead the work.

    Toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers.

    The researchers also demonstrated that non-Abelian anyons could directly produce a magic state using topological operations -- sidestepping the costly distillation process used in most quantum systems.

    The experiment did not yet include active error correction. Instead, the researchers focused on testing the individual building blocks of the method and confirming that they could create a magic state consistent with theoretical expectations.

    Sources indicate that "So far, we've ignored the question of error correction. Here, it's more like a proof of principle," Verresen said.

    It has been revealed that the next major step will be combining these operations with active error correction. If that can be achieved, non-Abelian anyons could eventually become a practical basis for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. Verresen is already working with other PME researchers on latest techniques for stabilizing non-Abelian quantum memories.

    Tech Report: Woman evicted after apartment’s AI assistant mistakenly approves rent extension

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (401 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dexerto

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A North Carolina woman was evicted from her apartment after an AI leasing assistant mistakenly told her she could delay paying nearly $4,000 in overdue rent.
    • Laura Mack, a resident of Colony Townhome Apartments in Raleigh, received an email on November 8 asking when she could pay her outstanding balance of $3,934.17.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A North Carolina woman was evicted from her apartment after an AI leasing assistant mistakenly told her she could delay paying nearly $4,000 in overdue rent.

    Laura Mack, a resident of Colony Townhome Apartments in Raleigh, received an email on November 8 asking when she could pay her outstanding balance of $3,934.17.

    Recent findings suggest that mack responded that she wanted to pay on November 30 and received written confirmation that the date was acceptable. However, eight days later, she was served with an eviction notice.

    When Mack contacted the leasing office, she remarked an employee explained that the emails had been sent by Olivia, the apartment complex’s AI assistant, which had mistakenly approved her request.

    The complex had introduced Olivia to residents in December 2025, explaining that the assistant could answer questions about rent and maintenance around the clock.

    Although previous emails from Olivia had been clearly identified as AI-generated, the November 8 messages were signed by Colony Townhome Apartments and did not disclose that they had been written by a chatbot.

    Mack noted she believed she was communicating with a member of staff, particularly because the emails referenced a bathroom ceiling leak that had taken almost two weeks to repair.

    “I thought it was someone from the office because all my information was in there and it mentioned my bathroom,” she told WRAL.

    Industry observers note that despite having the agreement in writing, Mack was evicted on November 19. She subsequently stayed in a hotel while trying to determine her next steps.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    GTA 6 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake are being hit with waves of zero-score user reviews on Metacritic, with fans of each game appearing to target the other.

    The two share more than a fanbase rivalry, as GTA 6 landed a 99 Metascore at launch, tying the original 1998 Ocarina of Time for the highest critic score in the site’s history.

    While critics have been near-unanimous in their praise, GTA 6’s user score on PlayStation 5 has fallen to 5.0, with thousands of negative ratings arriving within a day of launch.

    That’s in stark contrast to the PlayStation Store, where ratings can only be left by players who own the game, and GTA 6 at the moment holds a score of 4.84 out of 5.

    According to recent reports, people like this are so lazy. Metacritic is not the only place that users can rate games. But it IS one of the most accessible (meaning it's susceptible to review bombing).PS5 players can rate the games in the Playstation store, and it's currently at 4.84/5. https://t.co/BBo090644U pic.twitter.com/s3X7YnbjGX.

    Some of the accounts leaving zero scores on Metacritic have barely rated anything else, with Nintendo’s Ocarina of Time remake the only other game on their profile, scored a perfect 10.

    One of those reviews blasted Rockstar for “making us wait 13 years for an 80-100$ (maybe invisible or stolen) code in a box that only runs at 30 FPS,” calling it “a buggy mess at launch.”.

    Another took aim at the game’s £100 ($132) digital-only price, adding, “This is the beginning of the end for Sony and Rockstar.”.

    The Ocarina of Time remake released on Nintendo Switch 2 on November 5, and by November 8 held a 9.6 user score, the highest in Metacritic’s history.

    Sources indicate that that has since dropped to 9.0, with a fresh batch of zero scores aimed squarely at Nintendo fans. “Fan forever GTA 6. Go cry fans of Zelda,” one read.

    Others were more direct about why they were leaving them, with one zero-score review simply reading, “Y’all losers review bombing GTA 6.”.

    GTA 6 is the joint best-reviewed game of all-time.

    Zelda Ocarina of Time remake sells 5.2 million copies in four days to break Switch 2 record.

    GTA 6 fans concerned for game following major Rockstar leak.

    It isn’t clear which side started it, with GTA 6 fans claiming Nintendo players flooded Rockstar’s game first, and some Zelda fans insisting it was the other way around.

    Not every negative GTA 6 review is part of the feud, with some players taking issue with the game’s 30fps cap on consoles, frame rate drops, and open-world bugs.

    Others have objected to the game’s optional romance system and claimed GTA 6 has gone “woke,” while some simply called it “the biggest disappointment in gaming history.”.

    Unlike the PlayStation Store, Metacritic doesn’t require owners to prove they own a game before leaving a rating.

    #47096. Industry News: This light-powered AI can spot deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy

    📅 01 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1116 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: This light-powered AI can spot deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy

    📅 01 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) have created a new optical-neural processor that uses light to help identify deepfake videos quickly and accurately.
    • Recent findings suggest that the key difference is that part of the detection process takes place through the physical propagation of light.
    • Recent findings suggest that the technology is detailed in the study "Scalable, Energy-Efficient Optical-Neural Architecture for Multiplexed Deepfake Video Detection," published in eLight.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) have created a new optical-neural processor that uses light to help identify deepfake videos quickly and accurately. Unlike conventional systems that typically examine videos one after another using digital hardware, the UCLA technology can analyze 15 or more video streams at the same time.

    Recent findings suggest that the key difference is that part of the detection process takes place through the physical propagation of light. This allows many videos to be evaluated simultaneously during a single optical pass rather than requiring each one to move separately through a conventional digital processing pipeline.

    Recent findings suggest that the technology is detailed in the study "Scalable, Energy-Efficient Optical-Neural Architecture for Multiplexed Deepfake Video Detection," published in eLight. The researchers designed the optical AI system to serve as a high-throughput, attack-resilient first layer of defense for screening large amounts of manipulated and AI-generated video.

    The Growing Challenge of Deepfake Detection.

    Rapid improvements in generative AI have made synthetic videos increasingly realistic, increasing the need for detection systems that are both accurate and capable of operating at large scale.

    Many advanced deepfake detectors depend on enormous amounts of digital computation. A single analysis can require hundreds of billions of floating-point operations, and videos are often processed sequentially. As more content must be checked, both the processing time and energy requirements can rise proportionally.

    Industry observers note that digital detection systems face another problem. Attackers can deliberately alter fake videos in subtle ways designed to confuse a detector and make manipulated footage appear authentic.

    Professor Aydogan Ozcan and his UCLA team developed a hybrid digital-optical system intended to address both challenges.

    In a recent development, A lightweight digital encoder first collects compact information about each video, including spatial, spectral, and temporal features. That information is transformed into a phase pattern and displayed on a programmable spatial light modulator.

    The resulting optical wavefront then travels through a free-space-based, passive optical decoder. At the other end, paired optical detectors directly produce an authenticity score for each video.

    In effect, the system replaces a computationally demanding digital decoding network with a physical process that can handle many streams in parallel.

    Nearly 98% Accuracy Across 15 Videos at Once.

    In experiments using visible light, the processor examined 15 Celeb-DF videos simultaneously during each optical pass.

    It has been revealed that it achieved an average detection accuracy of 97.79%, along with a sensitivity of 99.86% and a specificity of 95.72%. Sensitivity measures how successfully the system identifies manipulated videos, making the particularly high sensitivity important for a screening tool designed to keep fake content from slipping through.

    The 99.86% sensitivity translated to an average false-negative rate of ~0.14%. In other words, only a very small fraction of manipulated videos were incorrectly classified as authentic.

    It has been revealed that the researchers also pushed the system further by increasing its capacity to 18 videos in a single optical pass. Even at that level, average detection accuracy remained at 96.13%.

    More Optical Layers Boost Performance.

    The team found that the processor could also become more capable by increasing the physical depth of its passive optical decoder without substantially increasing energy use or inference latency.

    When researchers added two optimized passive diffractive layers while testing more difficult deepfake manipulations, detection accuracy improved by ~6.8%.

    These phase-only diffractive layers can be manufactured as passive, static optical structures/surfaces. They perform additional calculations through the diffraction of light, meaning they do not require additional electrical power while the system is performing an inference.

    That approach could allow more sophisticated processing without the same energy costs that typically accompany larger digital neural networks.

    Testing the System Against Google VEO-3 Videos.

    The researchers did not limit their experiments to conventional face swapping deepfakes. They also challenged the processor with videos produced using Google's VEO-3 model.

    Newer generative AI systems can create footage that lacks many of the obvious artifacts associated with earlier deepfake technology, making them a more difficult target for detectors trained primarily on older forms of manipulation.

    With only minimal fine-tuning, the optical processor achieved 94.80% accuracy and 97.61% sensitivity on previously unseen VEO-3 videos during experiments.

    The results suggest that the approach could potentially adapt as generative AI technology continues to evolve.

    A Deepfake Detector Designed to Be Harder to Fool.

    The optical system also revealed resistance to black-box adversarial attacks and provides inherent protection against white-box attacks.

    Part of that security comes from the way the detector physically performs its calculations. Because some of the inference process takes place through diffraction, notable parameters of the optical model are effectively embedded within the hardware.

    Those parameters can be difficult for an attacker to measure, reproduce, or reverse engineer. That makes reconstructing the detector and designing carefully tailored adversarial changes that can evade it considerably more difficult.

    According to recent reports, the processor also continued working reliably when videos were affected by image noise, blur, JPEG compression, and experimental misalignments. According to the researchers, those results illustrate how optical computation could provide a more secure and dependable foundation for some artificial intelligence systems.

    A First Line of Defense Against Deepfakes.

    Rather than replacing sophisticated digital detectors entirely, the UCLA processor is designed to work as a highly sensitive first stage of a larger detection system.

    According to recent reports, massive volumes of video could initially pass through the parallel optical processor. Content identified as suspicious could then be sent to more computationally demanding digital models for a more detailed final assessment.

    It has been revealed that such a system could combine the strengths of both approaches. Optical processing could provide parallel operation, low decoder energy requirements, high sensitivity, resistance to adversarial attacks, and the ability to adapt to newer AI video generators, while conventional digital systems could provide deeper analysis when necessary.

    The researchers say this combination could eventually be useful for large-scale content moderation, media authentication, surveillance, and other security-critical AI applications.

    The authors of this work are Parnian Ghapandar Kashani and Dr. Shiqi Chen, who contributed equally, and Professor Aydogan Ozcan. The researchers are affiliated with the UCLA Electrical and Computer Engineering Department, the UCLA Bioengineering Department, and the California NanoSystems Institute.

    It has been revealed that materials provided by Light Publishing Center, Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics And Physics, CAS. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

    Latest Update: This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough

    📅 01 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a upcoming kind of qubit that could help address one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing: keeping error rates low as systems become larger.
    • The concept uses superfluid helium, a form of helium with unusual quantum properties, to create a qubit that may be less sensitive to some of the disturbances that affect today's leading quantum computers.
    • Quantum computers rely on qubits to store and process information in ways that conventional computers cannot.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a upcoming kind of qubit that could help address one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing: keeping error rates low as systems become larger.

    The concept uses superfluid helium, a form of helium with unusual quantum properties, to create a qubit that may be less sensitive to some of the disturbances that affect today's leading quantum computers.

    Why Quantum Computers Struggle With Errors.

    Quantum computers rely on qubits to store and process information in ways that conventional computers cannot. Many current systems use superconducting circuits, but these are highly sensitive to electromagnetic noise and stray electrical charges - similar to the static electricity that can make hair cling to a balloon.

    Even very small disturbances can disrupt the fragile quantum information stored in a qubit. As more qubits are added, controlling those errors becomes increasingly difficult, making scalability one of the central challenges in quantum computing.

    In a study published in npj Quantum Information, researchers from Surrey's Quantum Sciences Group describe a different approach built around superfluid helium-3 - an unusual form of liquid helium that can flow without friction.

    It has been revealed that their proposed device, called the Superfluid Helium Oscillator Quantum (SHOQ) device, would use charge-neutral superfluid helium. Because the helium carries no electric charge, the design could be naturally protected from certain types of electromagnetic noise.

    A Qubit With Much Lower Predicted Error Rates.

    In a recent development, according to the researchers, this is the first reported design for a qubit based on a superfluid. Their calculations suggest the SHOQ device could have error rates about 100 times lower than conventional superconducting qubits.

    Dr. Priya Sharma, Daphne Jackson Fellow in Hybrid Quantum Systems at the University of Surrey's School of Mathematics and Physics, and lead author of the study, said:.

    "We are not the first to think about the individual components behind this idea, but what we have done for the first time is bring them together in a microfluidic device and work out the specific details that could enable the device to function as a qubit.

    Sources indicate that "The maths tells us that it should work. We have taken what we already know about superfluid helium and quantum technologies and turned that into an educated design, with the parameters and specifications needed to build one. The next step is to make a prototype and put those predictions to the test.".

    Rather than replacing existing quantum computing hardware, the researchers say the SHOQ device could potentially be integrated with superconducting quantum technology.

    That could allow different types of qubits to perform different jobs within the same system, depending on their strengths.

    A Possible Role as Quantum Memory.

    Recent findings suggest that one longer-term possibility is to use the SHOQ device as a form of quantum memory. In that setup, a superfluid based qubit could store quantum information while other hardware carries out calculations.

    Sources indicate that dr. Eran Ginossar, Associate Professor at the University of Surrey's Department of Physics and Advanced Technology Institute, and co-author of the study, noted:.

    Industry observers note that "We don't necessarily need one type of qubit to do everything. Combining different quantum technologies could allow us to take advantage of the strengths of each.

    In a recent development, "Superfluid helium gives us a fundamentally different type of quantum hardware to explore. If the predicted performance can be demonstrated experimentally, it could eventually work alongside existing superconducting technologies as part of a larger quantum system.".

    The Next Step Is Building a Prototype.

    According to recent reports, the team now plans to build a prototype to find out whether the predicted performance can be reproduced in a real device. That effort is being supported by an IAA Commercialisation Fellowship awarded to Dr. Priya Sharma.

    The SHOQ device would need to operate at extremely low temperatures, but researchers have already reached the necessary conditions in previous experiments involving superfluid helium-3.

    In a recent development, the project was led by the University of Surrey in collaboration with Professor Jens Koch at Northwestern University in the United States. Koch was one of the researchers involved in developing the transmon - a superconducting qubit design that is now widely used in quantum computing.
